newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Schiphol efficiency boost likely following agreement.
newsitem.headline: Schiphol efficiency boost likely following agreement.

text.p: Dutch air freight handling companies, airlines and forwarders are tring to resolve a dispute about charges which should improve efficiency at Schiphol, said Hans Knuvers, secretary of the Air Transport Association of the Netherlands (ATAN).
A solution has been reached which aims to standardise a 'Ready for Carriage' system for all companies bringing airfreight to the leading Dutch airport, he told Reuters in an interview.

NVLA, the trade association for airfreight ground handlers and NVVL, the Dutch airfreight forwarders association, worked with ACAN, the trade body for 50 of the top airlines at Schiphol airport, to find a solution to 'zendinggeld' - a system of charges which are estimated to have cost shippers between five and eight million Guilders a year.
ATAN, the umbrella trade association for the Dutch air freight sector, co-ordinated a lengthy round of talks last year aimed at abolishing the levy system.

The levy is charged by cargo handlers and forwarders for receiving air freight as it arrives at the airport for onward despatch. The system has no equivalent at other European airports, and is held by shippers to be unfair.

Knuvers said all parties had worked hard to find a specific definition of the term 'Ready for Carriage.' "It is an IATA term, but in fact there's no specific IATA definition of its meaning. There are many different interpretations of Ready for Carriage."
Over the next six months, all related parties at Schiphol will prepare to remove charges for good.

"Until July 1 1997 the levy remains, but we will work with new pro-forma documentation and build up to the second part of the year when the charge will be dropped. However, after that time, consignments that do not comply with the 'ready for carriage' conditions will face a charge," Knuvers stated.
A new standard system will be introduced, which Knuvers believes will be the first of its kind in use anywhere in the world.

"We have made a long list of technical specifications, and we have created a fundamental definition of Ready for Carriage, which means consignments must be delivered to ground handlers' warehouses, pre-packaged, complete with an air way bill with customs clearance, and the consignment must comply with the booking made in advance of its arrival on the warehouse floor," he said.
"The other alternative is for freight to be positioned on the ramp of a lorry to enable a fork lift truck with short forks to remove it."
The new agreement has had to be extremely specific in its instructions.

"In the absence of an international definition of Ready for Carriage, we think it is important to get it right. As far as we know this is the first time 'Ready for Carriage' is defined, properly, with a standard goods receipt and guidelines on how to bring cargo to an airline."

"There are principally two parties involved: shipper and airline, yet it is extremely rare for the shipper to bring its goods to an airline: there are so many other parties in the loop: forwarders, agents, ground handlers, road haulage companies - the list goes on and on," he noted.

"At the end of the day we're hopeful that this will increase efficiency: there's a chance for time and money savings. Teething problems are always possible in the first six months trial period, but the ultimate goal is to achieve more efficiency, so yes, there's a strong possibility for savings," Knuvers said. -- Air Cargo Newsroom Tel+44 171 542 7706 Fax+44 171 542 5017
